/-!
# Erdős Problem 48

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/48](https://www.erdosproblems.com/48)
-/

@[expose] public section

open scoped ArithmeticFunction.sigma

namespace Erdos48

/--
Are there infinitely many integers $n, m$ such that $ϕ(n) = σ(m)$?
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos48.lean#L599"]
theorem erdos_48 :
    answer(True) ↔ {(n, m) : ℕ × ℕ | n.totient = σ 1 m}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos48

reformulations.difference: Lean allows zero in both coordinates, whereas the arithmetic functions in the source are ordinarily considered on positive integers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Nat.totient n = 0 iff n = 0, and σ 1 m = 0 iff m = 0. Thus the natural-number solution set is exactly the positive-integer solution set with the single pair (0,0) inserted. Inserting one element preserves infinitude. This equivalence, including the surrounding True ↔ statements, was proved in /workspace/review/scratch.lean without invoking the sorry-backed theorem.
